provider_readback.text:
How does a spider breathe underwater?

The diving bell spider (*Argyroneta aquatica*) builds a web-supported pocket of air under freshwater. It replenishes the pocket from the surface, but the remarkable part is what happens between those trips: oxygen dissolved in the surrounding water can diffuse into the bell. That makes the air-water boundary a physical gill.

Seymour and Hetz measured oxygen and gas conductance in laboratory diving bells. Many bells supplied enough oxygen for resting spiders in warm, still aquarium water. But nitrogen leaves the chamber, so it gradually shrinks and the spider still needs fresh air eventually. These tests do not establish oxygen supply during all activity or in every natural habitat.

TT-006 | Seymour & Hetz (2011), Journal of Experimental Biology, DOI: 10.1242/jeb.056093
Full source, methods, limitations and media credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-006.html

Real spider reference photographs (not the experiment): bykovskii and Lennart Lennuk, CC BY 4.0, cropped/graded; source/licence links on research page. Gas-transfer and measurement sequences are original conceptual illustrations, not recorded data. Synthetic narration. Official Toxic Tales logo.

provider_readback.text:
Do bumblebees play? Look at these rolling balls.

In a laboratory, *Bombus terrestris* repeatedly manipulated small wooden balls, even though no nectar or pollen reward was attached. Researchers provided a clear route to food, so bees did not need to move the objects to feed. Younger bees rolled balls more often than older bees in a separate test. In another experiment, a chamber colour previously associated with rolling influenced their later choices, even when the balls were absent.

These findings support interpreting the behaviour as play-like or intrinsically rewarding. They do NOT directly establish how a bee feels, whether the activity improves future skills, or how often wild bees do this.

TT-007 | Galpayage Dona et al. (2022), Animal Behaviour 194:239–251. DOI: 10.1016/j.anbehav.2022.08.013
Methods, evidence and full visual credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-007.html

Original experimental footage: Galpayage Dona and colleagues, CC BY 4.0, edited from Supplementary Video S1; natural-history photos Marco Almbauer and Aethonatic, CC0, reference only. Conceptual diagrams are original illustrations. The 11-of-13 young-bee count comes from the paper's separate laboratory age test; its animation reveals that fixed result, not a measured time series. Synthetic narration; official Toxic Tales logo.

Why would a bumblebee roll a wooden ball when there is no food reward?

In laboratory experiments, Bombus terrestris bumblebees repeatedly rolled balls despite having a clear route to food. In a separate age test, younger bees rolled more often. A colour-chamber experiment also suggested that the activity itself could be rewarding.

The researchers interpreted the behaviour as play-like. These laboratory tests do not directly reveal how bees feel or establish how often wild bees do this. The age and colour tests used separate experimental groups.

provider_readback.text:
A fish that spits its answer: can archerfish tell human faces apart?

In two laboratory experiments, separate groups of four Toxotes chatareus learned which face image earned food and which to avoid. During testing, the familiar unrewarded face was paired with one new face at a time, drawn from a pool of 44 images in the first experiment. The fish discriminated above chance.

Four different fish also succeeded with 18 novel faces after colour, mean brightness and the outer head outline were standardized. Only TWO faces appeared per trial. The results show learned image discrimination; they do not demonstrate that fish recognise their owners or use the same cues as humans.

TT-008 | Newport, Wallis, Reshitnyk & Siebeck (2016), Scientific Reports 6:27523. DOI: 10.1038/srep27523
Paper, methods, limitations and full credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-008.html

Archerfish reference photograph: Reichenthal, Ben-Tov & Segev (2018), Front. Neural Circuits 12:18, Fig.1A, CC BY 4.0, cropped; from a separate study (10.3389/fncir.2018.00018). Original conceptual task illustrations, not actual face-test footage or stimuli. Synthetic narration; official Toxic Tales logo.

#ToxicTales #Archerfish #AnimalBehaviour #FishCognition #Ecology #ScienceCommunication
